global.headline: BESSENT SAYS US-IRAN HORMUZ DEAL COULD COME 'TODAY OR TOMORROW' AS OIL PLUNGES, BUT TEHRAN DENIES DIRECT TALKS
summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday there was "a chance we may have a deal today or tomorrow to open the strait and move towards a more normalised position in this conflict," describing an emerging arrangement under which ships would enter the Persian Gulf via an Iranian-controlled route and exit via an Omani one, with Iran barred from charging a toll — "I think it would be freedom of movement," he said. Secretary of State Marco Rubio struck a more cautious note, telling reporters "there's been progress made in those talks, but not finality yet," while reiterating Washington's rejection of any deal giving Iran supervisory control of the strait. The optimism sits awkwardly against Monday's clash, in which Trump branded Tehran "extremely duplicitous" after Iran's foreign ministry said it was holding no direct talks with the US at all — only Oman-mediated talks on a shipping route. Iranian spokesman Esmail Baghaei repeated that position Tuesday: "We are not currently holding negotiations with the United States. Our talks are with Oman."

Oil swung sharply on the mixed signals: Brent crude fell $3.95, or 4.72%, to $79.82 a barrel by mid-afternoon GMT Tuesday, having earlier traded as high as $86.33 and briefly touching $79.73 — around 5% down on the day — though its failure to break decisively below $80 suggested traders were not yet ready to fully price out the war's risk premium.

The war's toll on US readiness came into sharper focus Tuesday: CNN reported that the US military has burned through nearly 80% of its pre-war THAAD interceptor inventory and roughly half its Patriot interceptors since fighting resumed, with fewer than 827 Patriot and 278 THAAD interceptors now left in stockpile and senior commanders warning the reserve is "dangerously low" — a shortage analysts say could take years to rebuild and could constrain readiness for any future conflict with China, Russia or North Korea. The broader shipping crisis the Hormuz talks are meant to resolve remained live: an India-flagged cargo vessel, MSV Faize Noore Oliya, capsized and sank Tuesday after being hit by a projectile in Yemeni waters; all 14 crew, including 13 Indians, were rescued by the Yemeni coast guard and taken to the port of Mokha, and India's foreign ministry condemned the attack.
global.geopolitical: The gap between Bessent's upbeat "today or tomorrow" framing, Rubio's guarded "progress but not finality," and Iran's flat denial of any US channel shows the diplomatic track remains contested even inside the US administration's own messaging, while the interceptor-stockpile disclosure adds a harder constraint: Washington may now have a material incentive, beyond midterm politics, to wind the war down before its own missile-defence reserves are further depleted.
global.socioeconomic: A near-5% intraday swing in Brent on a single Treasury Secretary's comment underscores how thin the market's confidence in any deal still is; a genuine Hormuz reopening would meaningfully ease fuel and freight costs for import-dependent economies, but the strait's continued vulnerability — illustrated by Tuesday's sinking of an Indian-flagged vessel off Yemen — means shippers have little reason yet to price in a durable resolution.

global.headline: GAZA HOLDS MASS FUNERAL FOR 112 BODIES FINALLY RECOVERED FROM 2023 SABRA STRIKE
summary: Palestinians gathered Tuesday for a mass funeral for more than 100 bodies recovered from the rubble of a November 2023 Israeli strike that flattened a residential block in Gaza City's Sabra neighbourhood, killing 308 members of two extended families, including 40 children, 30 women and seven people with disabilities, according to Palestinian officials. Gaza's Civil Defence began sifting through the rubble only last month; dozens of victims had never been recovered until now. The remains of the 112 identified Tuesday were wrapped in Palestinian flags and laid in rows among the ruins for funeral prayers, with hundreds of mourners, some standing atop the rubble itself, before the bodies were carried by stretcher along a street lined with destroyed buildings and buried nearby.
global.geopolitical: That a strike from nearly three years ago is only now yielding a body count shows how far Gaza's reckoning with the war's human cost lags behind its diplomatic timeline — the Hamas disarmament process and ceasefire-implementation talks are proceeding on a calendar of weeks, even as basic accounting for civilian deaths from earlier in the war is still being completed in real time.
global.socioeconomic: Diverting Gaza's severely under-resourced Civil Defence teams to slow, manual rubble-clearing for recovery rather than reconstruction illustrates how thinly stretched the territory's capacity remains nearly three years on, with recovery work of this kind competing directly against rebuilding housing, water and health infrastructure for the living.

global.headline: RUSSIAN DRONE 'SAFARI' HUNTS KHERSON VENDOR AS UKRAINE'S WILDBERRIES STRIKES KILL FIVE IN MOSCOW REGION
summary: Ukraine's foreign minister Andrii Sybiha accused Russia of a war crime after video circulated Tuesday showing a Russian drone chasing a street vendor around his stall in Kherson before exploding; the man, in his 50s, survived with shock and shrapnel injuries. President Volodymyr Zelensky called it part of a "drone safari" against civilians — a documented pattern, dating to May 2024, in which Russian drone operators have hunted individual Ukrainian civilians in and around Kherson, which a UN commission has already found constitutes crimes against humanity and war crimes.

Overnight, Ukraine struck back at Russian commercial infrastructure: drones hit multiple warehouses, including two run by online retailer Wildberries, in the Moscow, Leningrad and Tver regions. Moscow region governor Andrei Vorobyov said the strike on an industrial zone in the Chekhov district killed five people and injured ten. Ukraine has now hit nearly two dozen Wildberries logistics sites since mid-July, accusing the retailer of supplying the Russian military with drone components.
global.geopolitical: Both incidents point to a war in its fifth year eroding the line between civilian and military targets from opposite directions — Russia's sustained, UN-documented targeting of individual Ukrainian civilians for what monitors describe as psychological terror, against Ukraine's expanding campaign against Russian commercial logistics it says have become militarily useful — with neither side showing appetite to pull back.
global.socioeconomic: Repeated strikes on Wildberries, one of Russia's largest online retailers, are starting to disrupt ordinary Russian consumer logistics rather than purely military supply chains, while the normalisation of drone attacks on individual civilians going about daily commerce in Kherson keeps deepening the economic paralysis of front-line Ukrainian towns.

global.headline: GUATEMALA'S FUEGO VOLCANO ENTERS 'CRITICAL EXPLOSIVE PHASE,' FORCING MASS EVACUATIONS
summary: Guatemala raised its volcanic alert to the second-highest level Tuesday after the Fuego volcano entered its most explosive "paroxysm" phase late Monday, a state authorities say could last 24 to 72 hours. At least 1,421 people have been evacuated, including entire hamlets — El Porvenir and Las Lajitas, in San Juan Alotenango, Sacatepéquez — as pyroclastic flows roll down the volcano's surrounding ravines and lava fountains light up its slopes. Ash has spread as far as 120km, reaching heights above 5,000 metres, with more than 29,000 people affected by ashfall and an aviation alert warning pilots of contaminated airspace west and south-west of the volcano, extending to the Mexican border.
global.geopolitical: Fuego's eruptions periodically test Guatemala's disaster-response coordination with Mexico and other Central American neighbours on aviation and ashfall warnings, in a region where the volcano's 2018 eruption — which killed more than 190 people — still shapes how seriously evacuation orders are taken and complied with.
global.socioeconomic: Ashfall affecting nearly 30,000 people threatens crops and livestock across a heavily agricultural area around the volcano, while the evacuation of entire hamlets for what could be a multi-day paroxysm imposes shelter and disruption costs on communities already living with Fuego's near-constant background activity.

global.headline: EU MINISTERS DECLARE 'FULL SOLIDARITY' WITH SPAIN AFTER CEUTA CRISIS, SEEK TO COOL TENSIONS
summary: EU interior ministers held an emergency video call Tuesday on the aftermath of last week's roughly 70,000-person crossing into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, with Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner declaring the bloc's "full solidarity" with Spain and calling the episode "a test of our European resilience." Brunner said the EU's migration system had ultimately worked: "when it mattered, the situation was brought under control," with Spain saying about 70,000 of the 72,000 people who entered have already been returned to Morocco. The call, chaired by Ireland's EU presidency, was aimed explicitly at lowering the "political temperature" after Spain publicly rebuked Italy and Denmark's push for the meeting as "selfish, polarising and unlawful," even as 22 other EU leaders had separately called for tougher measures against "uncontrolled mass crossings."
global.geopolitical: A meeting billed as emergency coordination produced mostly reassurance rather than new mechanisms, suggesting the EU is choosing to paper over the intra-bloc rift Ceuta exposed — between states demanding harder deterrence and Spain defending its rapid-return approach — rather than resolve the underlying disagreement over how migration surges should be shared or managed.
global.socioeconomic: Framing the crisis as already resolved via mass returns to Morocco reinforces the EU's reliance on third-country cooperation to manage migration pressure at its external border, a dependency that keeps costs and responsibility concentrated on Morocco and on Spain's own reception capacity rather than being distributed EU-wide.

singapore.headline: PARLIAMENT PASSES TOUGHER TRAFFIC LAWS TARGETING DRINK DRIVING, PHONE USE AND ROGUE MOTORISTS
summary: Parliament passed the Road Traffic (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill on Tuesday, introduced by the Ministry of Home Affairs on 7 July amid a roughly 24% rise in Singapore's traffic fatality rate and a roughly 38% rise in traffic violations between 2021 and 2025. The most-debated change makes merely holding a mobile phone while driving an offence — previously, prosecutors had to prove the device was being actively used — punishable by up to S$1,000 or six months' jail for a first offence and up to S$2,000 or a year's jail for repeat offenders; hands-free calls or navigation via a properly mounted device remain permitted. The Bill also tightens penalties for drink and drug driving and introduces harsher provisions for repeat and dangerous offenders. MPs voiced strong support during the debate, with some calling for even harsher penalties than those proposed.
singapore.geopolitical: Criminalising mere possession of a phone while driving, rather than requiring proof of active use, is a stricter standard than most regional peers currently apply, positioning Singapore's amendments as a possible template other Asia-Pacific jurisdictions wrestling with similar enforcement gaps may look to.
singapore.socioeconomic: The changes raise compliance stakes for delivery riders, private-hire drivers and logistics firms whose work depends on phone use en route, adding pressure to adopt mounted-device workflows even as the tougher drink- and drug-driving penalties are aimed squarely at reversing the recent rise in fatal accidents.

singapore.headline: ONG YE KUNG: 11 OTHER MOH PROJECTS BESIDES NATIONAL CANCER CENTRE HAD UNDECLARED SAVINGS
summary: Health Minister Ong Ye Kung told Parliament on Tuesday that the non-declaration of project savings flagged by the Auditor-General's Office in the National Cancer Centre Singapore building project was not an isolated case, saying the Ministry of Health "did not declare savings for all its development projects, and not just for the one we audited" — extending the lapse to 11 other MOH developments. The AGO's report had found MOH left S$147.96 million in savings undeclared and called S$30.83 million in tenders before formal approval on the cancer-centre project, which was planned from 2013 and completed in 2022 with eventual savings of S$105 million; auditors separately found MOH used S$11.95 million of the undeclared savings on three items without Finance Ministry approval, two of them (worth S$4.08 million) having previously been rejected. Ong maintained there was no deliberate wrongdoing, saying the savings arose from lower tender prices and were redirected to needs such as a pedestrian link bridge connecting the cancer centre to Outram Park MRT station.
singapore.geopolitical: Confirming the lapse spans a dozen projects rather than one keeps Singapore's public-sector financial-governance practices under sharper domestic parliamentary scrutiny, in a system regional governments often cite as a benchmark for probity even though this case concerns process non-disclosure rather than any allegation of graft.
singapore.socioeconomic: With multibillion-dollar healthcare infrastructure spending set to keep rising alongside an ageing population, a finding that savings-declaration lapses were systemic rather than isolated is likely to sharpen calls for tighter financial-reporting discipline across statutory boards managing major public building projects.

singapore.headline: ARREST WARRANT ISSUED FOR OPPOSITION LAWYER LIM TEAN AFTER HE FAILS TO SURRENDER FOR JAIL TERM
summary: An arrest warrant was issued for lawyer and Peoples Voice party chief Lim Tean, 61, after he failed to surrender at the State Courts on Monday to begin a three-month-and-a-week jail sentence. Lim was convicted in July 2024 on three charges under the Legal Profession Act for continuing to appear in court and file documents on 32 occasions in 2021 despite holding no valid practising certificate; his original six-week sentence was enhanced on appeal in February 2026, and the Court of Appeal rejected a further bid to challenge the enhanced term in July. He had already been granted one deferment, from 20 July to 3 August, before failing to appear a second time. A warrant-of-arrest review has been scheduled for 17 August.
singapore.geopolitical: The case tests Singapore's legal-profession discipline and enforcement of court orders against a prominent opposition-aligned lawyer at the same time as a separate Law Society bid to have Workers' Party chief Pritam Singh struck off works through the courts, keeping the judiciary's handling of politically visible legal figures under sustained public attention.
singapore.socioeconomic: Repeated deferments followed by a failure to surrender risk being read as a public figure delaying accountability rather than an isolated lapse, a perception that could affect Lim's standing with existing clients and his own legal practice regardless of the warrant's eventual outcome.

word.definition: A sudden, violent attack or outburst — a sharp intensification of an emotion, activity or condition, often followed by a return to calm.
word.etymology: From Greek paroxysmos ("irritation, exasperation"), from paroxynein ("to goad, sharpen"), from para- ("beside, alongside") plus oxynein ("to sharpen"), itself from oxys ("sharp"); it entered English via Late Latin paroxysmus in the medical sense of a fit or attack of disease, before broadening by the 17th century to any sudden violent outburst.
word.example: Guatemalan authorities said Fuego had entered its most explosive "paroxysm" phase late Monday, a term borrowed from volcanology for a sudden violent intensification that, by Tuesday, could just as easily have described a war lurching between talk of a Hormuz deal and a fresh strike sinking a ship off Yemen.
